title: 2026-10-22_Sandworm_Exaramel_Incident_Response_Scenario_3d2
description: Investigate and respond to a security incident involving the Exaramel backdoor on a target system.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target system has exhibited unusual network activity and potential unauthorized access. Your task is to investigate and respond to this security incident.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system's IP address is `192.168.50.5`. Enter `start` to begin the scenario.
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario. You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system's IP address is `192.168.50.5`. Enter `start` to begin the scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Unusual Network Activity
levels.content: The target system has shown suspicious outbound network connections. Your task is to identify and investigate any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system.
levels.solution: Check the running services and network connections on the target system using commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` and `ss -tulnp`. The hidden flag is the name of the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the running services and network connections on the target system.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `ss -tulnp` to list network connections.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and examine their statuses.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Now that you have identified the suspicious service, you need to find out how it maintains persistence on the system. Investigate the persistence mechanisms used by the service.
levels.solution: Look for systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks that might be responsible for starting the suspicious service using commands like `systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled` and `crontab -l`. The hidden flag is the name of the persistence mechanism or the service unit file.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Look for systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks that might be responsible for starting the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled` to list enabled systemd services and `crontab -l` to list cron jobs.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled` to list enabled systemd services and examine their paths.

levels.title: Identify Lateral Movement
levels.content: Investigate any evidence of lateral movement from the target system to other systems in the network. Look for file transfers, remote execution, or other indicators of lateral movement.
levels.solution: Check the logs and systemd timers for any evidence of file transfers or remote execution using commands like `journalctl -xe` and `systemctl list-timers`. The hidden flag is the name of the service or script responsible for lateral movement.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Check the logs and systemd timers for any evidence of file transfers or remote execution.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use commands like `journalctl -xe` to view system logs and `systemctl list-timers` to list systemd timers.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: Try running `journalctl -xe` to view system logs and look for any unusual entries.
